pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 13: Test your theory on something that can't sue you.*

Toby unrolled a piece of parchment on the wobbly flowerpot table, where he had drawn a grid with a ruler. "We need data," he announced, adjusting his gold-rimmed glasses. "Marnie, grow the pea plant."

Marnie raised her wand. "Grow!"

The pea plant shuddered, and a single, damp, lavender-scented sock popped out of the soil to land directly on Toby’s shoe. The gold glitter wave, visible through the shed window, ignored it completely, keeping on rolling toward the village as if it had not noticed.

“Interesting,” Toby said, writing *Wonky magic = invisible to the hex* in his neat handwriting. “The inspectors cast one correct spell and were gnomed on the spot. You cast a wrong one and the hex does not even look up. It eats perfection. Wonky does not interest it.”

“So it is rude to be correct,” Lulu said very quietly, “and polite to be wrong.”

“It is a theory,” said Toby, and he underlined it twice.

Bunt sneezed, a tiny *ah-CHOO*, and the wave rippled but did not retreat, continuing its slow, steady approach.
pages.image: Inside a cluttered shed, four children observe a glowing gold wave outside the window; a small garden gnome stands frozen while a heap of mismatched socks piles up around its feet, and a boy in a vest writes on a chart.

pages.text:
The wave reached the bakery first. Mrs. Humphreys ran to the window, flour on her nose. "The bread is flat," she wailed. "It won’t rise! It’s just... bread."

Next, the lamppost at the corner of Crumb Lane tried to announce the time. It creaked, clicked, and fell silent. The village was losing its magic, one perfect little trick at a time.

Mayor Fenwick arrived in a puff of dusty wind. Her tall pink hat was straight, but her eyes were wide. She looked at the four of them, then at the creeping gold light.

"Can you fix it?" she asked. Her voice shook. "Please. With respect, given nobody else can."

Marnie looked at her hands. They were shaking. She looked at Bunt, who was holding a biscuit so tightly it was cracking. She looked at Lulu, who was hugging her knees.

"We don't know how," Marnie said.

But the wave was already licking at the bakery door. And the clock in the square had stopped ticking.
pages.image: A worried mayor in a tall pink hat stands before a flat loaf of bread and a silent lamppost, while a glowing gold wave creeps across the cobblestone street toward a small group of children.

pages.text:
"I have to tell you something," Marnie said. The words felt like a spoon stuck in the back of her throat. "The hat."

She told them about the rehearsal, the crooked tilt, the whisper, and the sudden *honk* that had silenced the Great Hall.

Silence stretched in the shed. It was the kind of quiet that happens right before a teacher asks a question nobody wants to answer. Gerald tilted his head, looking deeply offended at the mention of his former self.

Lulu reached out and squeezed Marnie’s hand. Her mismatched socks crunched on the straw. "I am so sorry," she said, though it wasn't her fault. "It is not your fault."

Toby pushed his glasses up his nose. His fingers were steady. "You made a wrong spell," he said carefully, ticking them off on his fingers. "Cassius made a bad plan. The Principal told a lie about the hat being ordinary. Everybody did one thing."

Bunt nodded slowly, his moss-green tuft bobbing. "Ah... yes. The hat was crooked. That was the school. Not you."

Marnie wanted to believe them. She wanted to believe that a sneeze wasn't a crime. But the gold wave was still glowing outside. And her hands were still shaking. And the memory of the goose landing in the punch bowl was brighter than the light.
pages.image: An eleven-year-old girl with copper-red hair in buns looks down sadly while a boy in a vest and a young troll offer comfort; Gerald with a purple ribbon watches with dignity in the background.

pages.text:
A squeaky voice cut through the guilt. Professor Quillfeather, the gnome librarian, waddled onto the table. She wore a tiny cardigan and spectacles so large they covered half her face, giving her the look of a confused owl who had just woken up in a library.

"Psst," she said, adjusting her glasses. "Do not cry. Crying ruins the ink."

She pointed a tiny, bony finger at the window. "The Founding Charter. Third shelf. Founders' Section. Great Library. There is an answer. There always is."

Marnie blinked. "The Great Library? It’s... it’s full of gnomes."

"Yes. And the hex is spreading." Quillfeather’s eyes were sharp. "By midnight, it will cross the lawn. Then it will be permanent. We are all going to become garden decorations, Miss Pennywhistle. I have a very nice spot in mind for myself, by the way. Near the ferns."

She hopped off the table. "Go. Hurry. I will keep the gnomes from waddling into the road. Try not to step on me."

The clock on the wall, the one that never ticked, seemed to hold its breath.
pages.image: A tiny owlish gnome librarian with large spectacles stands on a wooden table, pointing urgently out a window where a gold glow is visible, while three children look on in shock.

pages.text:
"Back way," Toby said, pulling a crumpled map from his vest. "Through the hedge, up the kitchen stairs, along the Longest Corridor."

Bunt began packing. He placed three sandwiches in his barrel-boot pocket, wrapped in wax paper. Lulu packed a bag of socks, just in case they needed to apologize to the furniture.

Marnie picked up Gerald. He squawked and tried to hide a stolen pencil under his wing. "Come on," she said. "We’re going to a library."

They stepped out into the twilight. The shadows of the school stretched long and thin across the glittering lawn, like fingers reaching for them. The Mayor stood at the gate, her hand raised in a stiff salute.

"Good luck," she whispered.

Marnie took a breath. The air smelled of lavender and impending doom. She walked forward, her red sneakers crunching on the gravel, and for the first time in two years, she didn't feel like a failure. She felt like a tool.
pages.image: Four children walk toward a dark school building at dusk, casting long shadows; the girl carries Gerald, and a figure in a pink hat salutes from the gate as a gold glow pulses behind them.
